claim: Endogenous sighs are generated periodically, typically every few minutes in rodents and humans.
source: Endogenous sighs generated periodically, typically every few minutes in rodents and humans, reinflate collapsed alveoli to maintain proper gas exchange in the mammalian lung (Knowlton and Larrabee, 1946; Mccutcheon, 1953; Reynolds, 1962).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research (Knowlton and Larrabee, 1946; Mccutcheon, 1953; Reynolds, 1962).

claim: Endogenous sighs reinflate collapsed alveoli to maintain proper gas exchange in the mammalian lung.
source: Endogenous sighs generated periodically, typically every few minutes in rodents and humans, reinflate collapsed alveoli to maintain proper gas exchange in the mammalian lung (Knowlton and Larrabee, 1946; Mccutcheon, 1953; Reynolds, 1962).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research (Knowlton and Larrabee, 1946; Mccutcheon, 1953; Reynolds, 1962).

claim: Two largely parallel medullary pathways from the pF to preBötC appear critical for the generation of physiological sighs.
source: Two largely parallel medullary pathways from the pF to preBötC appear critical for the generation of these physiological sighs: pF neurons expressing NMB or GRP project to preBötC neurons expressing their cognate receptors, NMBR and GRPR (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Li et al., 2016).

claim: pF neurons expressing NMB or GRP project to preBötC neurons expressing their cognate receptors, NMBR and GRPR.
source: Two largely parallel medullary pathways from the pF to preBötC appear critical for the generation of these physiological sighs: pF neurons expressing NMB or GRP project to preBötC neurons expressing their cognate receptors, NMBR and GRPR (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Li et al., 2016).

claim: The pF to preBötC pathways mediate confinement-induced claustrophobic sighing.
source: These pathways also appear to mediate confinement-induced claustrophobic sighing (Li et al., 2020), and by extension, other forms of sighing associated with emotional states such as during sadness, anxiety, depression, relief, or happiness (Ramirez, 2014; Li and Yackle, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Li et al., 2020).

claim: The pF to preBötC pathways mediate other forms of sighing associated with emotional states such as during sadness, anxiety, depression, relief, or happiness.
source: These pathways also appear to mediate confinement-induced claustrophobic sighing (Li et al., 2020), and by extension, other forms of sighing associated with emotional states such as during sadness, anxiety, depression, relief, or happiness (Ramirez, 2014; Li and Yackle, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research (Ramirez, 2014; Li and Yackle, 2017) and inference from the claustrophobic sighing finding.

claim: In rodents, the preBötC receives inputs from NMB and GRP pF neurons.
source: In rodents, the preBötC receives inputs from NMB and GRP pF neurons, and genetic deletion of NMBRs or GRPRs or local antagonism of NMBRs or GRPRs in preBötC significantly reduces endogenous sighing, while local injection into preBötC of bombesin, NMB or GRP significantly increases spontaneous sighing (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Li et al., 2016).

claim: Genetic deletion of NMBRs or GRPRs in preBötC significantly reduces endogenous sighing in rodents.
source: In rodents, the preBötC receives inputs from NMB and GRP pF neurons, and genetic deletion of NMBRs or GRPRs or local antagonism of NMBRs or GRPRs in preBötC significantly reduces endogenous sighing, while local injection into preBötC of bombesin, NMB or GRP significantly increases spontaneous sighing (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Li et al., 2016).

evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Li et al., 2016).

claim: Local injection into preBötC of bombesin, NMB or GRP significantly increases spontaneous sighing in rodents.
source: In rodents, the preBötC receives inputs from NMB and GRP pF neurons, and genetic deletion of NMBRs or GRPRs or local antagonism of NMBRs or GRPRs in preBötC significantly reduces endogenous sighing, while local injection into preBötC of bombesin, NMB or GRP significantly increases spontaneous sighing (Li et al., 2016).

claim: Bilateral pF long pulse photostimulation (LPP) in Grp-ChR2 mice elicits ectopic sighs that appear similar to endogenous sighs.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and described in the text.

claim: VT of ectopic sighs from pF Grp-ChR2 photostimulation were no different from endogenous sighs (n=4 mice).

evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: No sighs were generated by LPP in sigh phase 0.0–0.2 in Grp-ChR2 mice.
source: No sighs were generated by LPP in sigh phase 0.0–0.2 (34±5 s from previous sigh, measured from 30 stimuli in 5 mice: basal sigh rate 21±3 /hr, range 17–25; intersigh interval 172±25 s) in Grp-ChR2 and in phase 0.0–0.3 (58±20 s from previous sigh, measured from 48 stimulus in 4 mice: basal sigh rate 20±7 /hr, range 13–27; intersigh interval 193±65 s) in Nmb-ChR2 mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: No sighs were generated by LPP in sigh phase 0.0–0.3 in Nmb-ChR2 mice.
source: No sighs were generated by LPP in sigh phase 0.0–0.2 (34±5 s from previous sigh, measured from 30 stimuli in 5 mice: basal sigh rate 21±3 /hr, range 17–25; intersigh interval 172±25 s) in Grp-ChR2 and in phase 0.0–0.3 (58±20 s from previous sigh, measured from 48 stimulus in 4 mice: basal sigh rate 20±7 /hr, range 13–27; intersigh interval 193±65 s) in Nmb-ChR2 mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: In Grp-ChR2 mice, pF LPP did not elicit ectopic sighs when applied very shortly after an endogenous sigh (phase range: 0.0–0.2), indicating a postsigh refractory period for sigh induction.
source: Notably, in either Grp-ChR2 or Nmb-ChR2 mice, pF LPP did not elicit ectopic sighs when applied very shortly after an endogenous sigh (phase range: 0.0–0.2 and 0.0–0.3 of endogenous sigh cycle, respectively; Figure 1e), indicating a postsigh refractory period for sigh induction.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: In Nmb-ChR2 mice, pF LPP did not elicit ectopic sighs when applied very shortly after an endogenous sigh (phase range: 0.0–0.3), indicating a postsigh refractory period for sigh induction.
source: Notably, in either Grp-ChR2 or Nmb-ChR2 mice, pF LPP did not elicit ectopic sighs when applied very shortly after an endogenous sigh (phase range: 0.0–0.2 and 0.0–0.3 of endogenous sigh cycle, respectively; Figure 1e), indicating a postsigh refractory period for sigh induction.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The vast majority of Nmbr and Grpr cells (>97%) did not colocalize with the specific astrocytic marker Aldh1l1, indicating that these cells are neurons.
source: The vast majority of Nmbr and Grpr cells (>97%) did not colocalize with the specific astrocytic marker Aldh1l1, indicating that these cells are neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 57% of Nmbr neurons coexpressed Grpr.
source: In our sample, 57% of Nmbr neurons coexpressed Grpr, which constituted 32% of the Grpr population (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: Nmbr neurons that coexpressed Grpr constituted 32% of the Grpr population.
source: In our sample, 57% of Nmbr neurons coexpressed Grpr, which constituted 32% of the Grpr population (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: Approximately 85% of Nmbr and Grpr neurons co-expressed VGlut2.
source: Approximately 85% of Nmbr and Grpr neurons co-expressed VGlut2 (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: Approximately 10% of Nmbr and Grpr neurons colocalized with Sst.
source: Finally, we asked whether Nmbr and Grpr were expressed on preBötC Sst neurons. We found scant colocalization of Sst and Nmbr or Grpr (~10%), indicating that the substantial majority of these peptide receptors are not on Sst neurons (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: The substantial majority of Nmbr and Grpr receptors are not on Sst neurons.
source: Finally, we asked whether Nmbr and Grpr were expressed on preBötC Sst neurons. We found scant colocalization of Sst and Nmbr or Grpr (~10%), indicating that the substantial majority of these peptide receptors are not on Sst neurons (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Inference based on the low colocalization rate (~10%) observed in experimental data.

claim: preBötC LPP during 0.2–0.9 sigh phases elicited ectopic sighs in GrprFlp mice expressing ChR2 in preBötC GRPR neurons.
source: While no ectopic sighs could be generated by bilateral preBötC SPP in these mice (phase: 0.0–1.0), preBötC LPP during 0.2–0.9 sigh phases elicited ectopic sighs which appeared as partial doublet or augmented breaths, and reset the sigh cycle (Figure 3a, bottom).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Ectopic sighs elicited by preBötC LPP of GRPR neurons were no different from spontaneous sighs in VT and TE.
source: Ectopic sighs elicited by preBötC LPP of GRPR neurons were no different from spontaneous sighs in VT and TE (Figure 3b) and exhibited a postsigh apnea (TE following evoked sighs increased to 194 ± 22%, Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Ectopic sighs elicited by preBötC LPP of GRPR neurons exhibited a postsigh apnea (TE following evoked sighs increased to 194 ± 22%).
source: Ectopic sighs elicited by preBötC LPP of GRPR neurons were no different from spontaneous sighs in VT and TE (Figure 3b) and exhibited a postsigh apnea (TE following evoked sighs increased to 194 ± 22%, Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: preBötC LPP during 0.4–0.9 sigh phases elicited ectopic sighs in Nmbr-ChR2 mice.
source: Similarly, in Nmbr-ChR2 mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), preBötC SPP (phase: 0.0–1.0) had no effect on sighing, while LPP during 0.4–0.9 sigh phases elicited ectopic sighs which appeared as a partial doublet or an augmented breath, and reset the sigh cycle (Figure 3c, bottom).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: VT and postsigh TE of ectopic sighs elicited by preBötC LPP of NMBR neurons were no different from that of spontaneous sighs.
source: VT and postsigh TE of ectopic sighs were no different from that of spontaneous sighs (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Ectopic sighs elicited by preBötC LPP of NMBR neurons exhibited a postsigh apnea (postsigh TE increased to 225 ± 33%).
source: Ectopic sighs elicited by preBötC LPP of NMBR neurons exhibited a postsigh apnea (postsigh TE increased to 225 ± 33%, Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Latency from LPP to ectopic sigh onset was inversely related to phase in preBötC NMBR or GRPR neurons.
source: As with photostimulation of pF NMB and GRP neurons, there was a postsigh refractory period during which we could not generate ectopic sighs in preBötC NMBR or GRPR neurons. Again, the latency from LPP to ectopic sigh onset was inversely related to phase (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Application of CNO to the brainstem surface increased sigh frequency ~threefold in NmbrCre mice with preBötC NMBR neurons transduced with AAV-hM3Dq.
source: In these mice, application of the selective agonist clozapine-n-oxide (CNO) to the brainstem surface increased sigh frequency ~threefold (Figure 3f; see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for control CNO application).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Increasing the excitability of preBötC NMBR neurons increases sighing.
source: Thus, increasing the excitability of preBötC NMBR neurons increases sighing.
evidence: Inference based on the DREADD experiment results shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Only 3 of 21 preBötC GRPR neurons were inspiratory-modulated in Grpr-EGFP mice.
source: In Grpr-EGFP mice, only 3 of 21 preBötC GRPR neurons were inspiratory-modulated, i.e., fired during XII inspiratory bursts.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings.

claim: The majority of preBötC NMBR neurons (10/16) were inspiratory-modulated in Nmbr-tdTomato mice.
source: In contrast, in Nmbr-tdTomato mice, the majority of preBötC NMBR neurons (10/16) were inspiratory-modulated (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The majority of preBötC NMBR neurons (35/58; n=6) exhibited inspiratory-modulated Ca2+ oscillations coincident with XII bursts.
source: The majority of preBötC NMBR neurons (35/58; n=6) exhibited inspiratory-modulated Ca2+ oscillations coincident with XII bursts (Figure 4b); however, episodes of non-breathing-modulated episodic bursting, i.e., bursts not in phase with XII, were also seen (Figure 4c) and varied in frequency from 0.025 to 0.1 Hz (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Almost all NMBR neurons that had Ca2+ elevations during inspiratory bursts also had elevations during sighs (34/35).
source: Almost all NMBR neurons that had Ca2+ elevations during inspiratory bursts also had elevations during sighs (34/35), but not during the pre-I period, consistent with whole-cell recordings (Figure 4a), indicating that they are likely Type II, i.e., presumptive non-rhythm generating, neurons (Gray et al., 1999; Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging shown in Figure 4d.

claim: NMBR neurons are likely Type II, i.e., presumptive non-rhythm generating, neurons.
source: Almost all NMBR neurons that had Ca2+ elevations during inspiratory bursts also had elevations during sighs (34/35), but not during the pre-I period, consistent with whole-cell recordings (Figure 4a), indicating that they are likely Type II, i.e., presumptive non-rhythm generating, neurons (Gray et al., 1999; Figure 4d).
evidence: Inference based on the absence of pre-I activity and citation to prior research (Gray et al., 1999).

claim: The burst duration of the GCaMP6f signal associated with sighs was longer-lasting than those associated with eupneic events in the same neuron.
source: The burst duration of the GCaMP6f signal associated with sighs was longer-lasting than those associated with eupneic events in the same neuron (Figure 4d and e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d and e.

claim: NMBR neurons were still active during bursts but never during burstlets when [K+]ACSF was lowered to 6 mM.
source: We reliably observed both burstlets and bursts in population activity when we lowered [K+]ACSF to 6 mM (Shi et al., 2017). When we did so, NMBR neurons were still active during bursts but never during burstlets (Figure 4f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: When NMB (30 nM) was applied, only bursts were observed, while both burst and sigh frequency in both preBötC and XII increased.
source: When we applied NMB (30 nM), only bursts were observed, while both burst and sigh frequency in both preBötC and XII increased (Figure 4g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The percentage of sighs increased by 30% during NMB (30 nM) application in 6 mM K+.
source: The duration of sighs and eupneic bursts were similar in [K+]ACSF = 6 mM vs 9 mM (Figure 4h), while the percentage of sighs increased by 30% during NMB (30 nM) application in 6 mM K+ (Figure 4i), similar to the increase elicited by 30 nM NMB at 9 mM K+ 4.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: preBötC SPP of NMBR-only neurons elicited ectopic bursts which appeared similar to partial doublets or augmented breaths with smaller VT compared to spontaneous sighs due to a decrease in TI to 64 ± 8%.
source: When targeting NMBR-only neurons, preBötC SPP elicited ectopic bursts which appeared similar to partial doublets or augmented breaths with smaller VT compared to spontaneous sighs due to a decrease in TI to 64 ± 8% (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: TE immediately following SPP-induced ectopic bursts in NMBR-only neurons were longer than the TE of eupneic breaths.
source: TE immediately following these ectopic bursts were longer than the TE of eupneic breaths (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The time between the SPP-induced ectopic burst and the next endogenous sigh was shorter than the time between endogenous sighs, indicating that SPP-induced burst did not reset the sigh cycle.
source: Note that the time between the SPP-induced ectopic burst and the next endogenous sigh was shorter than the time between endogenous sighs, indicating that SPP-induced burst did not reset the sigh cycle (Figure 5b, top); SPP-induced ectopic burst could also occur in a sigh refractory period right after the previous eupneic sigh (Figure 5b, bottom).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: preBötC LPP in the late phase of the sigh cycle elicited ectopic sighs in GRPR-only neurons and reset the sigh cycle.

claim: Activation of either pF NMB or GRP neurons generates sufficient input to preBötC to generate ectopic sighs.
source: We conclude that: (i) activation of either pF NMB or GRP neurons generates sufficient input to preBötC to generate ectopic sighs; (ii) sighs can be generated by activation of preBötC GRPR and NMBR neurons even after blockade of NMBR and GRPR receptors; (iii) preBötC GRPR or NMBR neurons act via partially overlapping pathways to produce sighs via preBötC SST neurons; (iv) preBötC NMBR neurons are not rhythmogenic, and; (v) activation of preBötC SST neurons can generate sighs.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

evidence: Proposed mechanism based on experimental findings.

evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Del Negro et al., 2018).

evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Li et al., 2016).

claim: Sighs evoked by optogenetic stimulation of various preBötC subpopulations reset the sigh cycle and delayed the onset of the next endogenous sigh.

evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to prior research (Cui et al., 2016; Sherman et al., 2015; de Sousa Abreu et al., 2022).

claim: There is a postinspiratory refractory period in the respiratory cycle, during which ectopic breaths cannot be evoked immediately following termination of an inspiratory effort.
source: Also, similar to a postinspiratory refractory period in the respiratory cycle, during which ectopic breaths cannot be evoked immediately following termination of an inspiratory effort (Cui et al., 2016), we similarly observed a postsigh refractory period following an endogenous sigh, during which ectopic sighs could not be evoked.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Cui et al., 2016).

claim: There is a postsigh refractory period following an endogenous sigh, during which ectopic sighs could not be evoked.

evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: Vagotomy transiently abolishes eupneic sighs.
source: Although vagotomy transiently abolishes eupneic sighs (Cherniack et al., 1981), they can be evoked in the absence of sensory feedback in vivo after vagotomy Janczewski et al., 2012 or in vitro (Lieske et al., 2000; Feldman and Gray, 2000), suggesting that sensory inputs by themselves are not necessary, but likely modulate activity of these subpopulations to affect frequency of sighs.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Cherniack et al., 1981).

claim: Sighs can be evoked in the absence of sensory feedback in vivo after vagotomy or in vitro.

claim: Sensory inputs by themselves are not necessary for sighs, but likely modulate activity of these subpopulations to affect frequency of sighs.

claim: In mice, sigh-like movements appear in utero between E17 and E18.
source: In mice, sigh-like movements appear in utero between E17 and E18 (Chapuis et al., 2014), when at least two types of inspiratory-modulated neurons can be differentiated in rhythmic slices: neurons that fire in sync with regular 'eupneic' XII bursts, and those that fire only during sigh-like bursts (Chapuis et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research (Chapuis et al., 2014).

claim: At least two types of inspiratory-modulated neurons can be differentiated in rhythmic slices between E17 and E18: neurons that fire in sync with regular 'eupneic' XII bursts, and those that fire only during sigh-like bursts.

claim: Photoactivation of GRPR neurons had no effect on inspiratory burst amplitude.

claim: Microinjection of peptides NMB and GRP into preBötC increased sigh rate and inspiratory burst amplitude.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7g and h.
